quote: The fuels studied in these experiments were methanol and n-heptane. The droplets had initial diameters between 2 and 5 mm, and they were burned in oxidizing atmospheres at ambient temperature and various pressures between 0.70 and 3.05 atm, over ranges of dilution of oxygen with nitrogen, with carbon dioxide, and with mixtures thereof.
statement: FLEX burned methanol and n-heptane droplets of 2 to 5 mm initial diameter at ambient temperature, 0.70 to 3.05 atm, with oxygen diluted by nitrogen, carbon dioxide or mixtures.
limitations: Quiescent, spherically symmetric droplets; liquid fuels only.

quote: Burning rate—average burning rate constant from a linear fit of the droplet diameter squared versus time from shortly after ignition to extinction
statement: The FLEX 'burning rate' is the average burning-rate constant from a linear fit of droplet diameter squared versus time; Table IX reports it in mm2/s (the PSI-69 column header says 'mm').
limitations: Definition; resolves the PSI-69 unit label (see audit AUD-FLEX-UNIT).

quote: A principle objective was to determine the limiting oxygen index (LOI), the oxygen percentage below which combustion would not occur. This objective reflected the FLEX focus on investigating fire safety in spacecraft. Observed LOI values for these fuels appear to be slightly lower than initially expected.
statement: A main FLEX objective was the limiting oxygen index (the oxygen level below which combustion does not occur); observed values appeared slightly lower than initially expected.
limitations: Qualitative statement; the report does not interpret the data.

quote: Both radiative and diffusive extinctions occurred during the testing.
statement: Both radiative extinction (larger droplets, higher dilution) and diffusive extinction (smaller droplets) were observed in FLEX.

quote: (1) Burning-rate constants were average, and the droplet history was minimally influenced by the contaminant.
statement: A trace low-volatility contaminant was present in some FLEX tests; the authors judge burning-rate constants minimally influenced.
limitations: Known caveat carried into model cards.

quote: (4) Disruptive extinction of methanol is probably due to the presence of the contaminant.
statement: Disruptive extinction of methanol droplets is probably caused by the contaminant, so disruption outcomes should be treated cautiously.
limitations: Applies to disruption outcomes, not burning-rate constants.

quote: These extensive experimental results are not interpreted here; the intent is merely to make the data readily available for future scientific interpretation.
statement: The FLEX report catalogues more than 100 combustion histories without interpreting them.
limitations: Interpretation is left to users of the data.

quote: The objectives of these experiments are to (1) determine how rapidly a large scale fire grows in low-gravity and (2) investigate the low-g flammability limits compared to those obtained in NASA’s normal gravity material flammability screening test.
statement: Saffire aimed to measure how fast a large-scale fire grows in low gravity and to compare low-g flammability limits with NASA's 1-g screening test.

quote: The experiments will be conducted in Orbital ATK’s Cygnus vehicle after it has unberthed from the International Space Station.
statement: Saffire tests ran in an uncrewed Cygnus vehicle after it left the ISS, so large fires could be studied without risk to crew.

quote: I-1 Cotton-Fiberglass 40.6 cm 0.37 mm 94 cm 20 cm/s Concurrent 21.7 to 21.5
statement: Saffire-I sample I-1: a 40.6 cm wide, 0.37 mm cotton-fiberglass sheet in 20 cm/s concurrent flow at 21.5-21.7% O2 burned about 84 cm at 1.8 mm/s (Table 1).
limitations: Single test; cabin pressure not stated in the table.

statement: Saffire-I opposed-flow sample I-2 spread only about 10 cm, at 1.3 mm/s, over 70 s.
Saffire-II sample 2-5 (5 cm wide cotton-fiberglass, 20 cm/s concurrent, about 22.1% O2) burned its full 29 cm at 2.1 mm/s.
Saffire-II sample 2-6 (cotton-fiberglass) burned its full length at 2.6 mm/s. NTRS lists 25 cm/s flow; PSI-99 lists 20 cm/s (audit conflict).
limitations: Flow velocity disputed between sources; excluded from interpolation.

quote: 2-1 80 W 9.2 s Insignificant ~0 n/a ~ Complete Acceleratory
statement: Thin silicone samples showed insignificant burning in microgravity at 20 cm/s and about 22% O2, yet sample 2-1 burned roughly completely in the 1-g upward reference test.
limitations: One flow and O2 level; not proof of non-flammability elsewhere.

quote: 2-7 80 W 9.2 s 140 s 5 cm & 0 ii n/a (Nomex) ~ 0 (Nomex) n/a (Nomex)
statement: In the combined PMMA and Nomex sample 2-7, the PMMA section burned (5 cm) but the adjoining Nomex did not burn in microgravity.
limitations: One test and geometry; does not prove Nomex never ignites next to a burning material.

statement: Saffire-III large cotton-fiberglass sample 3-1 spread about 84 cm at 2.3 mm/s concurrent. NTRS lists 25 cm/s flow; PSI-100 lists 30 cm/s (audit conflict).
Saffire-III opposed-flow sample 3-2 spread about 10 cm at 0.98 mm/s.

quote: The Nomex sample did not ignite.
statement: On Saffire VI the Nomex fabric sample did not ignite.
limitations: One test; ignition conditions specific to the igniter used.

quote: The SIBAL sample (left image) achieved a steady size and spread rate quite rapidly where the two PMMA samples grew continuously until the flow speed was reduced.
statement: In Saffire VI the cotton-fiberglass sample reached a steady size and spread rate quickly, while the thick PMMA samples kept growing until flow speed was reduced.

quote: Overall, the temperature and pressure rise in the spacecraft were found to be less significant than the increase in carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide.
statement: Saffire IV-VI found the cabin temperature and pressure rise less significant than the increase in carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide.

quote: The lack of this experimental data has forced spacecraft designers to base their designs and safety precautions on 1-g understanding of flame spread, flame self-extinguishment, fire detection, and suppression.
statement: Without large-scale low-g data, spacecraft designers have relied on 1-g understanding of flame spread, self-extinguishment, detection and suppression.

quote: they were able to adapt to new flow variations such as blowoff extinctions, that proved to be very valuable data in outlining the U-shaped flammability boundary.
statement: BASS-II crew-adapted flow variations, including blowoff extinctions, helped outline a U-shaped flammability boundary versus flow.
limitations: Boundary shape, not a universal limit.

quote: for the microgravity tests presented herein, the flow velocities under investigation are near the quenching limit, below those normally expected from the air supply and recirculation systems currently employed on the ISS.
statement: BASS-II tested flows near the quenching limit, below those normally produced by ISS ventilation.

quote: Left: radiative quenching when flow velocity goes below 2 cm/s. Right: Flame nearing blow off extinction as the flow velocity crosses 40 cm/s. (0.1-mm-thick PMMA)
statement: For 0.1 mm PMMA, radiative quenching occurred below about 2 cm/s and blowoff extinction approached as flow crossed about 40 cm/s.
limitations: Image captions from a presentation (BASS-II heritage).

quote: Thin fuel sheets: few materials rated even in 1g at 34% O2, 8.2 psia (exploration atmosphere).
statement: Few thin-sheet materials are rated even in 1-g at 34% O2 and 8.2 psia, the proposed exploration atmosphere.

quote: Ignition and extinction maps of a solid fuel (PMMA cylinder) as a flow, O2, and external radiant flux.
statement: SoFIE objectives include ignition and extinction maps of PMMA cylinders versus flow, oxygen and external radiant flux.

quote: Theoretical and experimental results have demonstrated that some materials that will not burn in 1-g will burn in 0-g (with a low-speed flow) or in partial gravity (such as Lunar-g).
statement: Some materials that do not burn in 1-g can burn in 0-g with a low-speed flow, or in partial gravity such as Lunar gravity.

quote: Early numerical and experimental evidence suggested that Lunar gravity could be more hazardous, since flame spread rate as a function of gravity peaks there
statement: Early evidence suggested Lunar gravity could be more hazardous because flame spread rate versus gravity peaks near it.

quote: Flame base spread rate = .92 mm/s. • Flame tip spread rate = 1.1 mm/s
statement: On the LUCI rotating sounding rocket (simulated Lunar gravity), cotton-fiberglass fabric burning downward had a flame-base spread rate of 0.92 mm/s and flame-tip spread rate of 1.1 mm/s.
limitations: Single flight; Coriolis effects noted by the authors.

quote: Material flammability testing at partial-g is feasible using a spinning vehicle.
statement: LUCI showed material flammability testing at partial gravity is feasible on a spinning vehicle.

quote: The smoke was initially collected in an aging chamber to simulate the transport time from the smoke source to the detector.
statement: SAME-2 aged smoke in a chamber to simulate transport time from the source to the detector, varying it from 11 to 1800 s.

quote: The diagnostics included a prototype two-moment smoke detector and three different measures of moments of the particle size distribution.
statement: SAME-2 tested a prototype two-moment smoke detector and measured several moments of the particle size distribution.
limitations: Detector research, not a qualified system.

quote: riments performed to date demonstrated radiative and diffusive extinction, combustion instabilities, lower flammability limits and recently explained cool flame phenomenon after visible flame extinction.
statement: Droplet experiments demonstrated radiative and diffusive extinction, instabilities, lower flammability limits and cool flames after visible flame extinction.

quote: A snapshot of 2-cm diameter acrylic sphere burning in microgravity at 17 percent oxygen and 10 cm/s flow from the Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS) experiment
statement: BASS burned a 2 cm acrylic (PMMA) sphere in microgravity at 17% oxygen and 10 cm/s flow.

quote: The SPICE experiment investigated the transition from non-sooting to sooting
statement: SPICE investigated the transition of gas-jet flames from non-sooting to sooting.

quote: A sealed cabin, pressurized with an oxygen atmosphere. 2. An extensive distribution of combustible materials in the cabin.
statement: The Apollo 204 board listed conditions that led to the disaster, including a sealed oxygen-pressurized cabin and extensive combustible materials.

quote: Tests in a 16.5 psia oxygen atmosphere have shown that sparks blown from arcs can ignite combustible material several inches from the arc.
statement: Tests in a 16.5 psia oxygen atmosphere showed sparks from electrical arcs can ignite combustibles several inches away.

quote: Solid combustible materials used in the C/M includes plastics in the nylon, polyurethane and silicone rubber class.
statement: Solid combustibles in the Apollo command module included nylon, polyurethane and silicone rubber plastics.

quote: Pressure was rapidly lost in SM oxygen tank no. 2 and fuel cells 1 and 3 current dropped to zero due to loss of their oxygen supply.
statement: On Apollo 13, service module oxygen tank no. 2 lost pressure rapidly and two fuel cells lost their oxygen supply, leading to mission abort.
limitations: Pressurised cryogenic oxygen tank, not a cabin fire.

quote: as Lazutkin activated a solid-fuel oxygen generator in Mir’s Kvant-1 module, the canister ignited, shooting a three-foot flame with sparks and bits of molten metal across the module and generating a large quantity of dense smoke. The flame blocked the evacuation route to the Soyuz
statement: In 1997 a solid-fuel oxygen generator canister on Mir ignited, producing a three-foot flame, dense smoke, and blocking the route to a Soyuz escape vehicle.

quote: They identified the most likely culprit as latex working glove material inadvertently introduced into the canister.
statement: Investigators identified latex glove material introduced into the canister as the most likely cause of the Mir fire.

quote: The crew quickly donned oxygen masks, and Korzun began dousing the flame with foam from a fire extinguisher
statement: The Mir crew donned oxygen masks and used foam fire extinguishers.
